posts.topic: New build inspections: the three windows buyers skip
posts.hook: I've seen 47 defects in a house nobody lived in.

scores.worst_problem: The hook's most arresting detail (47 defects, nobody lived there) is spent verbatim as slide 3's payoff, so the deck's biggest reveal lands as a repeat rather than a punch.
scores.fix: Keep the 47-defect line on slide 3 and rewrite slide 1 with a different withheld detail from the same story (e.g. "The worst house I ever inspected had never been slept in.") so the reveal still pays off.

posts.topic: Why transplants quit Texas (month nine)
posts.hook: Transplants don't leave over the heat. Month nine does it.

scores.worst_problem: The final point slide's loop, "Most buyers get this backwards," promises a reveal that the deck never delivers — it swipes into the CTA question instead of an answer, leaving one loop dangling.
scores.fix: Rewrite slide 6's loop so it hands off to the closing question rather than teasing new information — e.g. "One trade-off decides it" — and sharpen slide 2's vague "Then the counting starts" into something that names what gets counted.

posts.topic: 19 months before the business paid me (delayed payoff, discipline)
posts.hook: My real estate business paid me nothing for 19 months. I almost quit in month seven.

deck.topic: 19 months before the business paid me (delayed payoff, discipline)
deck.hook: My real estate business paid me nothing for 19 months. I almost quit in month seven.

points.title: Month Seven, Broke
body: Savings gone. I took a warehouse shift four nights a week.
I told nobody in the business.
points.loop: That shift bought me something else.

points.title: The Shift Bought Time
body: With rent covered, I could say no to bad clients.
A desperate agent chases everything and closes nothing.
points.loop: The next rule was harder.

points.title: I Paid Myself Last
body: I picked one fixed number for my life and lived on it.
Everything above that went straight back into the business.
points.loop: But I stopped tracking income.

points.title: I Tracked Conversations
body: Ten real conversations a day. Not posts. Not likes.
Closings follow conversations. They just do not follow fast.
points.loop: The delay has a length.

points.title: About Nine Months
body: The work you do today pays out roughly nine months later.
So a slow month is a report card on last spring.
points.loop: Then month 19 happened.

points.title: Month 19
body: Three closings in one month, all from calls I made in month ten.
Nothing changed in month 19. Everything changed nine months before it.
points.loop: Nobody claps for month ten.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who is nine months into something and has not seen a dollar yet.

scores.worst_problem: Two of the six loops — "The next rule was harder" and "Then month 19 happened" — are filler transitions rather than teases; the latter re-announces information the hook already gave away.
scores.fix: Rewrite the weak loops to withhold a specific new thing, e.g. replace "The next rule was harder" with "Then I cut my own pay" and "Then month 19 happened" with "Three closings, one month, zero new work."

posts.topic: Texas toll roads: the $312 first month
posts.hook: I spent $312 on tolls my first month in Dallas. I never saw a toll booth.

deck.topic: Texas toll roads: the $312 first month
deck.hook: I spent $312 on tolls my first month in Dallas. I never saw a toll booth.

points.title: No Booths, Just Cameras
body: There is nowhere to stop and pay.
A camera reads your plate at highway speed and the bill shows up weeks later.
points.loop: Not every bill finds the driver.

points.title: The Plate Pays, Not You
body: The charge goes to whoever owns the car.
Rental cars, moving trucks, a friend's SUV. Rental companies stack a daily fee on top of the toll.
points.loop: Two neighbours can pay different rates.

points.title: Tag Or No Tag
body: With a toll tag you get the lower rate.
Without one you pay the mail rate plus a fee on every invoice. Same road, same miles, bigger bill.
points.loop: The price can move by the hour.

points.title: Lanes That Reprice
body: Around Dallas and Fort Worth, some lanes cost more as traffic builds.
The sign price climbs all afternoon. The same twelve miles can triple by five.
points.loop: Your city decides most of this.

points.title: Austin, Dallas, San Antonio
body: Austin is ringed with toll roads. Dallas is stitched with them.
San Antonio has almost none. Same commute length, very different monthly cost.
points.loop: Mine added up faster than expected.

points.title: How I Hit $312
body: Thirty one days of commuting, no tag, and one week in a rental.
Mail rate on every trip, plus a fee on every invoice. A tag and one route change would have cut it close to half.
points.loop: It changed which route I drive.

cta.question: Toll road every day, or 15 extra minutes on the free route?

scores.worst_problem: The final point's loop, "It changed which route I drive," is a soft summary rather than a tease, so the swipe into the close loses tension.
scores.fix: Rewrite the last loop as a forward-pointing tease that sets up the choice, e.g. "The free route costs something too."

posts.topic: Why agents go broke after their best year (commission money habits)
posts.hook: The agents I watch quit in Texas usually had their best year right before.

deck.topic: Why agents go broke after their best year (commission money habits)
deck.hook: The agents I watch quit in Texas usually had their best year right before.

points.title: The Best Year Trap
body: A big year changes what you spend. It does not promise another big year.
So the car, the office, the lifestyle all get set at a level one good stretch paid for.
points.loop: The spending outlives the year.

points.title: Commission Is Not Salary
body: One closing check is usually three months of work landing on a single day.
Spend it like a paycheck and you just spent a quarter of the year in three weeks.
points.loop: And one bill is already waiting.

points.title: Nobody Withholds Your Taxes
body: No employer takes anything out first. The whole check hits your account and none of it is fully yours.
I move a third into a separate account the day it lands.
points.loop: The timing is what actually hurts.

points.title: Your Work Pays 90 Days Late
body: The calls I make this week close in the spring. A quiet week today costs me nothing today.
It costs me a quarter from now, when I have forgotten why.
points.loop: Your bills run on a different clock.

points.title: Run On Your Worst Month
body: I set my fixed costs against my slowest month, not my average one.
Everything above that line is optional money, and it gets a job before it gets spent.
points.loop: You find out in year three.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who just had their biggest month and already upgraded the car.

scores.worst_problem: The hook's word order creates a garden-path stumble ('The agents I watch quit in Texas') and never names what kind of agents, forcing a reread on the one slide that can't afford one.
scores.fix: Rewrite slide 1 as a clean subject-first sentence, e.g. 'Most real estate agents who quit in Texas had their best year right before they walked away.', and replace the restating loop 'The spending outlives the year' with a forward tease like 'Then the checks stop matching.'

posts.topic: Price cut vs seller credit in the current Texas market
posts.hook: Texas sellers are cutting prices right now. Asking for the price cut is usually the wrong move.

deck.topic: Price cut vs seller credit in the current Texas market
deck.hook: Texas sellers are cutting prices right now. Asking for the price cut is usually the wrong move.

points.title: Homes Are Sitting
body: Across most Texas metros, houses are taking longer to sell than they did last spring.
Sellers who priced like it was 2022 are watching their listing get older every week.
points.loop: That changes their answer.

points.title: The Price Cut Trap
body: Buyers ask for money off the price because it sounds like the biggest win.
Spread across 30 years, a small price cut barely moves what you pay every month.
points.loop: Point it somewhere better.

points.title: Same 9,000 Dollars
body: Knock 9,000 off the price and your monthly change is pocket change.
Ask for that same 9,000 toward your rate instead and the monthly drop is far bigger.
points.loop: Most buyers never run both.

points.title: Sellers Prefer This
body: A price cut lowers the number every neighbor and every future appraiser sees.
A credit at closing keeps their sale price on paper, so they agree faster.
points.loop: But there is a ceiling here.

points.title: Know The Cap
body: Your loan type limits how much a seller is allowed to hand you.
Ask above that limit and the extra money just disappears at the table.
points.loop: Most buyers guess this wrong.

cta.payoff: the full payment breakdown showing what a price cut and a rate credit each do to your monthly number

scores.worst_problem: The loop on slide 1 ("That changes their answer.") is ambiguous — no question has been posed, so "their answer" points at nothing, and the final loop ("Most buyers guess this wrong.") reuses the same construction as slide 3's loop, blunting both.
scores.fix: Rewrite slide 1's loop to name the stake concretely (e.g. "So ask for this instead") and vary the closing loop so it doesn't echo "Most buyers never run both."

posts.topic: Builder contracts strip five buyer protections
posts.hook: Signing a builder's contract in Texas quietly removes five protections you think you already have.

deck.topic: Builder contracts strip five buyer protections
deck.hook: Signing a builder's contract in Texas quietly removes five protections you think you already have.

points.title: Your Option Period Shrinks
body: The standard Texas contract buys you days to inspect and walk away for a small fee.
Builder contracts often give you a short review window and no exit at all.
points.loop: The deposit part is worse.

points.title: Earnest Money Gets Big
body: Resale deals usually run about 1 percent down at signing.
Builders often want 5 percent or more, and it goes nonrefundable much sooner.
points.loop: Appraisals are where it stings.

points.title: No Appraisal Protection
body: If the house appraises under your contract price, you cover that gap in cash.
Walk away instead and the builder usually keeps what you put down.
points.loop: Your closing date isn't yours either.

points.title: Closing Date Is Theirs
body: Most builder contracts let them push the finish date back, sometimes by months.
Your rate lock expires and your lease ends. Neither of those is their problem.
points.loop: There's a fifth one buried.

points.title: The Clause In The Back
body: Nearly every builder contract sends disputes to arbitration instead of a courtroom.
Their own warranty replaces what you'd normally get, and most of it runs out fast.
points.loop: One kind of home flips this.

cta.payoff: the current new builds list with the already-finished homes flagged

scores.worst_problem: The map slide immediately names all five items the hook withheld, deflating the curiosity gap the hook just opened and leaving only 'the buried fifth clause' as real pull.
scores.fix: Rewrite the map so at least three entries are consequence-framed teases rather than plain labels (e.g. 'The 5% you can't get back'), so the reader still has to swipe to learn what each protection actually is.

posts.topic: The Austin to San Antonio I-35 drive nobody warns transplants about
posts.hook: Austin to San Antonio is 80 miles. Locals still block out three hours each way.

deck.topic: The Austin to San Antonio I-35 drive nobody warns transplants about
deck.hook: Austin to San Antonio is 80 miles. Locals still block out three hours each way.

points.title: The 80 Mile Lie
body: I-35 between the two cities has been under construction for years.
The map says 80 minutes. On a bad afternoon it is three hours each way, and there is no way around it once you are in it.
points.loop: Direction matters more than distance.

points.title: Direction Decides Your Day
body: Living in San Antonio and working in Austin is a completely different drive than doing it the other way.
The heavy morning wave runs north. Drive south instead and you can save half an hour on the same road.
points.loop: One clock ruins both directions.

points.title: The 3PM Problem
body: Most Texas schools let out right around 3pm.
School traffic and the early highway wave land at the same time. Parents who planned to leave at 4 learn to leave at 2:15.
points.loop: Fridays follow a different rule.

points.title: The Friday Getaway
body: On Friday afternoon, both cities empty out toward the coast and the Hill Country at once.
Leave at 4 on a Friday and you are in line with everyone else who had the same idea.
points.loop: There is a quieter hour.

points.title: How Locals Beat It
body: People who do this drive often leave before 2 or after 7. Nothing in between.
They also pay for the toll loop east of Austin and never complain about it.
points.loop: Where you buy settles this.

cta.question: If you had to commute it: Austin side or San Antonio side?

scores.worst_problem: The last point slide's loop, "Where you buy settles this," promises a payoff the deck never delivers — the next slide is the CTA, so the reader is teased into a dead end.
scores.fix: Replace the final loop with a line that hands off to the question instead of promising more content, e.g. "So which side wins?", and fix the hook/slide-1 mismatch by making both say miles or both say minutes.

posts.topic: The nine boring years: holding one rental beat trading four
posts.hook: The people who built real money in Texas real estate spent nine years doing nothing.

deck.topic: The nine boring years: holding one rental beat trading four
deck.hook: The people who built real money in Texas real estate spent nine years doing nothing.

points.title: Nine Years, One House
body: A client bought one rental in 2013 and never bought another.
Nine years later she still owned it.
points.loop: Sitting still costs something.

points.title: Every Year Had An Exit
body: 2015 was a job offer in another state. 2018 was a headline saying the top was in.
2020 was a neighbor offering cash on the spot.
points.loop: One of those almost worked.

points.title: The Year It Cost Money
body: Roof and AC went out the same summer.
She wrote a check that wiped out two years of profit. She kept the house anyway.
points.loop: That check bought her something.

points.title: The Friends Who Traded
body: Two people I know bought and sold four times in that same stretch.
Every sale meant fees, taxes, and starting a new loan over.
points.loop: The fees were the small part.

points.title: What Actually Compounds
body: Her loan got smaller every month while the rent went up.
Nobody feels that happening. It only shows up at the end.
points.loop: Most people quit before that.

points.title: How She Sat Still
body: She kept six months of repair money in cash and stopped checking the value online.
Boredom is a lot cheaper than panic.
points.loop: Almost nobody makes it there.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who has been waiting for a better time to buy since 2019.

scores.worst_problem: A couple of slide loops lean on unspecified pronouns — "One of those almost worked" and "That check bought her something" — forcing a half-second of decoding about what 'worked' or what was 'bought'.
scores.fix: Name the referent in the vague loops, e.g. "The 2020 cash offer nearly won" and "That check bought nine years of rent", so the tease points at a concrete missing fact rather than an unnamed one.

posts.topic: The 11-month new build warranty window
posts.hook: Your Texas new build has a one year warranty. Most buyers waste 11 months of it.

deck.topic: The 11-month new build warranty window
deck.hook: Your Texas new build has a one year warranty. Most buyers waste 11 months of it.

points.title: The Clock Starts At Closing
body: Your builder warranty year begins the day you close, not the day you move in.
If you closed in March, most of your coverage is gone by next March.
points.loop: Not every item lasts that long.

points.title: Some Coverage Dies Early
body: Structural coverage can run for years. Cosmetic stuff often does not.
Nail pops, grout, paint and drywall cracks can fall off the list in the first 30 or 60 days.
points.loop: One word ends most claims.

points.title: That Word Is Settling
body: Report a crack and you will hear it is normal settling. Sometimes that is true.
Without a dated record and a photo, you have no way to argue it.
points.loop: When you call matters more.

points.title: Call In Month Eleven
body: Hire your own inspector at month 11 and walk the whole house again.
That leaves you weeks to file everything before the year runs out.
points.loop: How you report it matters.

points.title: Email, Never Phone
body: A call to the site super leaves no proof it ever happened.
Email each item with photos and a date, and keep every reply.
points.loop: Most buyers miss half the list.

scores.worst_problem: The hook's "waste 11 months of it" implies waiting is the error, but the deck's core advice is to deliberately act in month eleven — a small logical collision that makes the payoff feel like it contradicts the setup.
scores.fix: Reword the hook to "Your Texas new build has a one year warranty. Most buyers lose most of it without ever filing a claim." so it sets up, rather than fights, the month-eleven advice, and sharpen the flattest loop ("How you report it matters") into something with a concrete hint like "One channel kills claims."

posts.topic: Cedar fever: the winter allergy season that blindsides Texas transplants
posts.hook: Transplants in Austin and San Antonio get sick every January. It is not the flu.

deck.topic: Cedar fever: the winter allergy season that blindsides Texas transplants
deck.hook: Transplants in Austin and San Antonio get sick every January. It is not the flu.

points.title: One Tree Does This
body: Central Texas is covered in ashe juniper, which everyone here calls mountain cedar.
It releases pollen in the cold months, not the spring. Peak is mid December through February.
points.loop: The pollen counts tell you why.

points.title: The Numbers Are Insane
body: Most pollens peak somewhere around 1,500 grains.
On a bad cedar day around Austin and San Antonio, counts blow past 20,000. You can see the yellow haze come off the trees when the wind picks up.
points.loop: That is why people misdiagnose it.

points.title: It Copies The Flu
body: Body aches. Low fever. Total exhaustion. Sinus pressure that makes your teeth hurt.
Urgent care rooms here fill up in January with people who are sure they caught something.
points.loop: Your first winter is the worst one.

points.title: Year One Hits Hardest
body: Your body has never seen this pollen before, so the reaction is loud.
Most transplants tell me season two was easier and season three was manageable.
points.loop: Four habits cut it way down.

points.title: What Locals Actually Do
body: Windows stay shut on dry windy days after a cold front. That is when the trees dump.
Fresh filters in December. Shower and change clothes before bed. Start your medicine two weeks before you feel anything, not after.
points.loop: Location changes the dose completely.

points.title: It Depends Where You Land
body: The heaviest cedar sits in the Hill Country west of Austin and north of San Antonio.
DFW gets a fraction of it. Their rough stretch is spring, with oak and grass instead.
points.loop: Most buyers never think to ask.

cta.question: Cedar season in the Hill Country or spring pollen in DFW?

scores.worst_problem: The final loop 'Most buyers never think to ask' introduces a real-estate 'buyer' frame that appears nowhere else in the deck, so the last swipe lands on an unearned pivot.
scores.fix: Replace 'Most buyers never think to ask' with a loop that stays in the deck's own language, e.g. 'One question before you sign', and drop 'Save this for later' from the CTA so the either/or question stands alone.

posts.topic: Why the Texas average days on market number is misleading right now
posts.hook: The average Texas home sells in about 60 days. Almost no actual home does that.

deck.topic: Why the Texas average days on market number is misleading right now
deck.hook: The average Texas home sells in about 60 days. Almost no actual home does that.

points.title: The Average Is Fake
body: That 60 day number comes from fast sales and stale listings added together.
Barely any home in Texas actually sells on day 60.
points.loop: There are two piles.

points.title: Pile One Sells Fast
body: Homes priced at what the last three sales actually closed for are moving in about two weeks.
Clean, empty, photographed well, and priced under the neighbor who is still sitting.
points.loop: The other pile is bigger.

points.title: Pile Two Just Sits
body: Homes priced five percent over the comps are running past 100 days.
Buyers see the day count first and assume something is wrong with the house.
points.loop: Time is not the real cost.

points.title: The Price Cut Trap
body: Most sellers cut in small amounts, a few thousand at a time, once a month.
Three small cuts almost always net less than one honest price on day one.
points.loop: Buyers are reading those cuts.

points.title: Where Buyers Have Room
body: A home past 90 days is where you ask for closing costs, a rate buydown, or repairs.
Sellers in that pile stopped defending the price weeks ago.
points.loop: The numbers shifted again this month.

cta.payoff: this month's Texas market numbers, broken down by days on market and inventory

scores.worst_problem: The final point slide's loop, "The numbers shifted again this month," teases nothing in the deck — it is a vague pivot to the CTA rather than a genuine reason to swipe.
scores.fix: Replace that loop with a content tease that pays off in the close, e.g. "One pile is growing fast," so the CTA report answers a question the deck actually raised.

posts.topic: Why a fixed rate loan still has a rising monthly payment in year two (escrow reset)
posts.hook: Texas buyers lock a fixed rate and still get a payment increase in year two.

deck.topic: Why a fixed rate loan still has a rising monthly payment in year two (escrow reset)
deck.hook: Texas buyers lock a fixed rate and still get a payment increase in year two.

points.title: Your Rate Is Not Your Payment
body: A fixed rate only locks the loan part.
Property taxes and insurance ride in the same monthly draft.
points.loop: One of those three gets guessed.

points.title: The First Year Is A Guess
body: At closing, the lender estimates your tax bill.
On a new build they often use the value of an empty lot.
points.loop: The real bill arrives in October.

points.title: Year Two Reset
body: The county finally appraises the finished house.
Your escrow account comes up short by the whole difference.
points.loop: You pay that gap twice.

points.title: How The Gap Hits Twice
body: The lender collects the missed money, spread over the next twelve months.
It also raises the draft going forward to cover the correct tax bill.
points.loop: Something else renews every year too.

points.title: Insurance Renewal
body: Texas wind and hail premiums have been climbing fast.
When your policy renews higher, escrow adjusts again.
points.loop: The deadline is April 30.

points.title: File Your Homestead Exemption
body: It lowers the taxable value on your primary home.
It also caps how much that value can rise each year at 10 percent.
points.loop: The true number is knowable upfront.

cta.payoff: the full payment breakdown, with taxes and insurance included

scores.worst_problem: The DM payoff — "the full payment breakdown, with taxes and insurance included" — is a vague deliverable rather than a named, picturable artefact, so it reads like a soft offer to talk rather than a thing worth typing for.
scores.fix: Name the artefact and bound it, e.g. "Comment MATH and I'll DM you the Year-Two Escrow Worksheet: plug in your build's finished value and see the exact payment you'll be drafted in month 13" — and sharpen the slide-1 loop from "One of those three gets guessed" to something that names the three parts, like "Only one of the three is guessed."

posts.topic: Texas school district lines do not match city lines (DFW and Austin suburbs)
posts.hook: A Frisco address can land you in four different school districts. Most buyers find out late.

deck.topic: Texas school district lines do not match city lines (DFW and Austin suburbs)
deck.hook: A Frisco address can land you in four different school districts. Most buyers find out late.

points.title: One City, Four Districts
body: A Frisco address can sit in Frisco ISD, Lewisville ISD, Prosper ISD or Little Elm ISD.
Same city on your mail. Four different school systems.
points.loop: One street can split in two.

points.title: Your Address Decides
body: Schools are assigned by your exact address, not by your city and not by distance.
The campus you can see from the porch may not be the one your kid attends.
points.loop: The district rating hides more.

points.title: The A Is An Average
body: A district rating is the average of every campus inside it.
In one A rated district, individual campuses can run from A down to C.
points.loop: Even the right campus can move.

points.title: Boundaries Get Redrawn
body: Fast growing suburbs in DFW and Austin open new schools, then move kids over to fill them.
Your street can get reassigned while you are still living in the same house.
points.loop: There is a way out. It closes early.

points.title: Transfers Fill Up Fast
body: Most Texas districts let you request a transfer to a different campus.
The window usually opens in winter, and the campuses everyone wants hit capacity in weeks.
points.loop: Your buyer cares more than you did.

points.title: Buyers Pay For Zoning
body: Two nearly identical houses can sell for different money based on which campus they feed.
If your street gets rezoned, that premium walks over to the house behind you.
points.loop: Most buyers confirm their campus too late.

cta.question: Top rated campus or shorter commute?

scores.worst_problem: The closing question introduces "shorter commute," a tradeoff the deck never raised, so it reads bolted on rather than earned by the six slides that preceded it.
scores.fix: Replace the close with an either/or drawn from the deck itself — e.g. "Buy in the A district, or buy the A campus? One word." — and drop the competing "save this" ask.

posts.topic: The Friday number: tracking booked next steps instead of income
posts.hook: I run a real estate business. Every Friday I check one number. It is not income.

deck.topic: The Friday number: tracking booked next steps instead of income
deck.hook: I run a real estate business. Every Friday I check one number. It is not income.

points.title: Income Lies To You
body: The money that hits your account this month came from work you did about 90 days ago.
Judging today by it is like driving while staring in the rear view mirror.
points.loop: So I stopped keeping score that way.

points.title: The Friday Number
body: Every Friday I count how many conversations ended with a real date on my calendar.
Not calls made. Not coffees had. Actual next steps booked with a time on them.
points.loop: My first count embarrassed me.

points.title: Mine Started At Two
body: Two. After a week where I felt busy from morning to night.
I wrote it down anyway. Ugly numbers only start moving once you are willing to look at them.
points.loop: The count itself is not the point.

points.title: You Only Own The Input
body: Rates, inventory, what a seller does on a Tuesday. None of that is yours.
How many next steps you booked this week is entirely yours. So that is the thing I grade.
points.loop: It fixed a money problem too.

points.title: Pay Yourself On Purpose
body: Commission comes in lumps. Three closings in April and nothing until July.
I pay myself the same amount every month off a rolling average. The rest sits and waits.
points.loop: Then a week showed up empty.

points.title: The Zero Week
body: Some weeks the number is zero. I still write the zero down.
A run of zeros is information, not a verdict. Two strong weeks wipe them out completely.
points.loop: Most people quit one month early.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who checks their bank balance more often than their calendar.

scores.worst_problem: The final loop, "Most people quit one month early," opens a promise the deck never pays off — it leads straight into the CTA, so the last swipe delivers nothing.
scores.fix: Replace the last slide's loop with a line that resolves the deck and hands off to the share close (e.g. "Zero weeks are not the enemy — blind weeks are"), and sharpen slide 1's transition loop from "So I stopped keeping score that way" into a real tease like "I found a better number."

posts.topic: Finished spec homes cost less than the identical to-be-built new build
posts.hook: The finished Texas new build costs less than the identical one still on paper.

deck.topic: Finished spec homes cost less than the identical to-be-built new build
deck.hook: The finished Texas new build costs less than the identical one still on paper.

points.title: The Builder Is Paying Interest
body: A finished home was built with borrowed money.
Every month it sits empty, the builder pays for it.
A home on paper costs them nothing yet.
points.loop: Timing beats negotiating here.

points.title: Watch The Calendar
body: Builders report sales by the quarter.
The last two weeks of March, June, September and December are when unsold homes become a problem.
Same house, very different answer.
points.loop: The discount never touches the price.

points.title: They Will Not Cut The Sticker
body: Lowering the base price would drag down the value of every home they still have to sell.
So the money comes back as closing costs, a rate buydown, or a bigger credit at the table.
points.loop: You also skip one dreaded room.

points.title: No Design Center
body: In a to-be-built home you pick every finish and pay retail for all of it.
A finished home already has that package installed, wrapped inside the price.
points.loop: The bigger win is not money.

points.title: You Can Actually Close
body: A to-be-built home is a guess on a calendar. Delays push your rate lock and your lease.
A finished home closes in about 30 days.
points.loop: Most of these never get advertised.

cta.payoff: the current list of finished Texas new builds sitting unsold right now

scores.worst_problem: Slide 2's closing body line, "Same house, very different answer," is compressed into vagueness — answer to what question, from whom? — forcing a reread mid-deck.
scores.fix: Rewrite that line as a complete claim, e.g. "Ask for a concession on March 3rd and on March 28th and you get two different answers."

posts.topic: Watering your foundation: Texas clay soil and slab movement
posts.hook: Texans water the dirt around their house on purpose. Transplants think we are crazy.

deck.topic: Watering your foundation: Texas clay soil and slab movement
deck.hook: Texans water the dirt around their house on purpose. Transplants think we are crazy.

points.title: The Ground Moves
body: Most of DFW and San Antonio sits on clay, and a lot of east Austin does too.
Clay swells when it rains and shrinks hard when it bakes. Your slab rides on top of it.
points.loop: Your house warns you first.

points.title: Doors Stop Closing
body: A door that suddenly sticks in August. A hairline crack above a door frame. A gap at one window corner.
That is not the house settling in. That is the dirt under one side pulling down.
points.loop: The fix is embarrassingly cheap.

points.title: A Twelve Dollar Hose
body: Lay a soaker hose about eighteen inches out from the slab and run it all the way around.
Twenty minutes in the evening, a few times a week in summer. You want steady damp, not a swamp.
points.loop: Not every day is legal.

points.title: Watering Days Are Real
body: San Antonio runs stage restrictions most summers and they get enforced.
Austin and Dallas assign watering days by your address. Foundation soaker hoses usually get an exception, but you have to know your city's rule.
points.loop: Getting this wrong has a price.

points.title: The Repair Bill
body: Once piers are involved, Texas foundation work lands in five figures fast.
You also disclose it when you sell, and buyers knock it off the price twice over.
points.loop: Your yard has a culprit.

points.title: The Tree Nobody Blames
body: A big thirsty tree near the slab pulls water out of that clay faster than a hose puts it back.
Shade on one side dries the other side unevenly. That is how one corner drops while the rest stays put.
points.loop: Nobody likes the honest answer.

cta.question: Big oak close to the house: keep it or cut it?

scores.worst_problem: Two of the six loops ('Getting this wrong has a price', 'Nobody likes the honest answer') are vague cost/consequence filler that could sit under any slide in any deck, so they don't name a specific withheld thing to swipe for.
scores.fix: Replace the generic loops with concrete teases tied to the next slide's actual content — e.g. 'Piers start at five figures.' and 'The tree usually wins.' — and drop 'Save this for later' from the CTA so the keep-or-cut question is the only ask.

posts.topic: The pay lag in a new real estate business and the runway it takes to survive it
posts.hook: I made zero dollars in my first five months in real estate. Nothing was wrong.

deck.topic: The pay lag in a new real estate business and the runway it takes to survive it
deck.hook: I made zero dollars in my first five months in real estate. Nothing was wrong.

points.title: The Money Runs Late
body: A conversation in March turns into a signed contract in May.
That deal closes in June and the check clears in July.
points.loop: The delay does something to your head.

points.title: Zero Feels Like A Verdict
body: My first five months paid me nothing, and it felt like proof I was bad at this.
It was not proof. Month six paid me for all five of them.
points.loop: Most people never get to month six.

points.title: Fund Six Months, Not Two
body: Rent, gas, dues, insurance. Add it up and multiply by six.
Most people save eight weeks of that and call it betting on themselves.
points.loop: Runway buys something besides time.

points.title: You Get To Say No
body: With money in the bank I could turn down the client who wanted to list 40 percent over market.
Broke, I take that listing, spend my own cash on photos, and sit on it for six months.
points.loop: The reward for that shows up late.

points.title: Year Two Pays Twice
body: In year two you get paid for the work you did in year one, plus the work you are doing now.
Same hours. Double the income. Nothing about you changed.
points.loop: Almost nobody is still around to see it.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who is four months into something new and quietly doing the math on quitting.

scores.worst_problem: The hook's payoff is partly guessable — anyone who knows real estate immediately supplies "commission lag," which softens the pull of "Nothing was wrong."
scores.fix: Sharpen slide 1 to withhold something less inferable, e.g. "I made zero dollars in my first five months in real estate. Month six paid me for all five of them." so the gap becomes what changed rather than why the money was late.

posts.topic: Deep builder discounts on Texas new builds that sat empty for months, and what sitting does to a house
posts.hook: The biggest builder discounts in Texas right now are on homes that sat empty for months.

deck.topic: Deep builder discounts on Texas new builds that sat empty for months, and what sitting does to a house
deck.hook: The biggest builder discounts in Texas right now are on homes that sat empty for months.

points.title: Why It Is Cheap
body: Builders keep building even when buyer traffic drops.
Every finished house they still own costs them money every single month.
So the one that sat longest gets the deepest cut.
points.loop: Empty months leave marks.

points.title: A Summer With Nobody Home
body: Some builders run the AC in empty houses. Some set it at 85 and lock the door.
Texas humidity does the rest. Sticky doors, warped trim, mildew up in the attic.
points.loop: Heat is the visible part.

points.title: Pipes That Never Ran
body: Drain traps dry out when nobody uses a sink for half a year.
That is where a sewer smell in a brand new house comes from.
Cheap to fix. Awful to discover after you move in.
points.loop: Outside is worse.

points.title: The Yard Nobody Watered
body: Dead sod is cheap to replace. Sunken dirt against the slab is not.
A sprinkler system that never ran can hide broken heads and dry zones you inherit.
points.loop: One date matters more than the price.

points.title: When The Coverage Started
body: Parts of a builder warranty can start at completion, not at your closing.
If the house sat eight months, you may have far less coverage left than you think.
points.loop: None of this shows on a walkthrough.

cta.payoff: the new build inspection checklist I use on homes that have been sitting

scores.worst_problem: The hook states a fact that reads as good news rather than a withheld catch, so a reader can plausibly stop at 'discounts are on stale inventory' and feel informed without swiping.
scores.fix: Rewrite slide 1 to name the catch without revealing it, e.g. 'The biggest builder discounts in Texas are on homes that sat empty for months — and four things happen to a house in that time that no walkthrough will show you.'

posts.topic: Why appraisals lag the market: closed comps, the gap, and the Texas financing addendum
posts.hook: A Texas appraiser is not allowed to value your home off today's prices.

deck.topic: Why appraisals lag the market: closed comps, the gap, and the Texas financing addendum
deck.hook: A Texas appraiser is not allowed to value your home off today's prices.

points.title: Appraisers Look Backward
body: The appraiser values your house off homes that already closed.
Usually sales from the last three to six months.
points.loop: Those closed sales are older than they look.

points.title: A Closed Sale Is Old News
body: A home that closed last month went under contract about 45 days before that.
So a recent comp is really a two or three month old price.
points.loop: That lag decides who writes a check.

points.title: The Gap Lands On The Buyer
body: If prices moved up, the appraisal comes in under the contract price.
The lender only lends on the appraised number. The buyer covers the rest in cash.
points.loop: One paragraph decides if you can walk.

points.title: The Paragraph Nobody Reads
body: In Texas, the financing addendum sets whether a low appraisal lets the buyer out.
Sign that protection away and it is cash out of pocket or your deposit.
points.loop: Most buyers accept the number here.

points.title: You Can Push Back
body: Your agent can send the appraiser better sales and ask for a second look.
It only works with real closed sales, not opinions about the market.
points.loop: Finding those sales is the whole job.

cta.payoff: this month's market numbers, the closed sales an appraiser will actually count

scores.worst_problem: The loop on the addendum slide — "Most buyers accept the number here" — is vague about which number and which moment, so it teases nothing specific and the swipe momentum sags right before the payoff slide.
scores.fix: Rewrite that loop as a concrete tease pointing at the next slide, e.g. "But a low number is challengeable" or "Appraisals get overturned every week."

posts.topic: Texas hail season and what it does to roofs, insurance and transplants
posts.hook: Texas transplants brace for tornadoes. Hail is the thing that actually gets them.

deck.topic: Texas hail season and what it does to roofs, insurance and transplants
deck.hook: Texas transplants brace for tornadoes. Hail is the thing that actually gets them.

points.title: Spring Is The Season
body: The worst hail runs March through May.
DFW gets hit hardest, but Austin and San Antonio get their share.
By the time summer heat arrives, the risky window has mostly passed.
points.loop: The damage often hides.

points.title: You Cannot See It
body: Hail bruises shingles without breaking them.
From the ground your roof looks completely fine.
The leak shows up a year or two later.
points.loop: Then the bill surprises you.

points.title: Your Deductible Is A Percentage
body: Most Texas policies use a separate wind and hail deductible.
It is often 1 to 2 percent of what your home is insured for, not a flat amount.
On a normal Texas house that is thousands out of pocket before insurance pays anything.
points.loop: And the payout can shrink.

points.title: Roof Age Changes Everything
body: Once a roof passes a certain age, many carriers stop paying to replace it.
They pay what the worn out roof is worth today instead.
Ask the age of the roof before you write an offer, not after.
points.loop: Then the trucks show up.

points.title: The Knock At The Door
body: After a big storm, crews go street to street offering free inspections.
Some are excellent local roofers. Some follow storms across three states and vanish.
Check that they were working in Texas last year, not last week.
points.loop: Most learn this the expensive way.

cta.question: New roof already on it, or older roof and negotiate for one?

scores.worst_problem: The final point slide's loop, "Most learn this the expensive way," is a generic summary that teases nothing specific and gives no reason to swipe.
scores.fix: Replace that loop with a concrete forward tease tied to the close, e.g. "One question saves you thousands," and tighten the CTA to a cleaner either/or like "Buying: new roof, or discount for old?"

posts.topic: Paying yourself a fixed salary out of lumpy commission income
posts.hook: My real estate income is different every month. My paycheck is the same every month.

deck.topic: Paying yourself a fixed salary out of lumpy commission income
deck.hook: My real estate income is different every month. My paycheck is the same every month.

points.title: Money Lands In Clumps
body: Three closings can land in one week.
Then nothing for forty days.
Your rent does not care about that.
points.loop: The fix is boring.

points.title: One Account Catches It All
body: Every commission check goes into one business account.
I never spend directly out of it.
It is a holding tank, not a wallet.
points.loop: Then one number decides everything.

points.title: Pay Yourself Your Worst Month
body: I set my salary off my slowest quarter, not my best one.
Same amount hits my personal account on the same day.
It feels too small at first. That is the point.
points.loop: Something comes out before that.

points.title: Taxes Are Not Yours
body: Nobody withholds for you when you are self employed.
A cut of every check moves out the day it clears.
Agents who skip this get wrecked in April.
points.loop: Most people spend the rest.

points.title: The Extra Has A Job
body: Whatever is left builds a cushion until the account holds six months of salary.
After that it goes into the business or into property.
It never becomes a nicer car.
points.loop: That cushion does something specific.

points.title: It Buys You The Word No
body: A hungry agent takes every client and every bad deal.
A paid agent can walk away from the ones that will cost more than they pay.
That choice is where the real money starts.
points.loop: Most never get there.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who just went commission only and is already living off their best month.

scores.worst_problem: Two of the six loops ('That cushion does something specific.', 'Something comes out before that.') are content-free placeholders that announce a gap rather than name a specific tease, weakening the swipe momentum mid-deck.
scores.fix: Rewrite the vague loops with concrete nouns — e.g. 'Six months buys one word.' and 'The IRS gets paid first.' — so each tease points at a specific thing the next slide will deliver.

posts.topic: Why the pre-approval number is not an affordable budget
posts.hook: Your lender will approve you for a number the lender knows you cannot afford.

deck.topic: Why the pre-approval number is not an affordable budget
deck.hook: Your lender will approve you for a number the lender knows you cannot afford.

points.title: Approval Is A Ceiling
body: A pre-approval says the bank believes the loan gets repaid.
It says nothing about the life you want to keep living.
points.loop: The first gap is in your paycheck.

points.title: They Use Gross Pay
body: The math runs on your income before taxes come out.
You make the payment with what actually lands in the account.
points.loop: Then they stretch that number further.

points.title: The 45 Percent Line
body: Most loan programs let your total debts reach around 45 percent of gross income.
That is a ceiling built for the bank, not a target built for you.
points.loop: Half your real bills never get counted.

points.title: The Invisible Bills
body: Daycare, groceries, gas, power, savings, travel. None of it shows on a credit report.
The bank cannot see any of it. You still pay all of it.
points.loop: Texas adds one more weight.

points.title: Taxes And Insurance
body: Texas property tax and home insurance run high compared to most states.
Both live inside the monthly payment, and neither one is locked in.
points.loop: One number sorts all of this out.

cta.payoff: the full payment breakdown for a Texas home, line by line, at the price you are actually looking at

scores.worst_problem: The hook's withheld piece is too guessable — anyone who has shopped a mortgage can predict 'because they use gross income,' which the very next slides confirm, so the gap closes before the swipe.
scores.fix: Sharpen slide 1 to withhold a specific, unguessable number or moment (e.g. 'Your lender will approve you for a payment that eats 45% of a paycheck you never actually see') so the reader wants the exact mechanism, not a category they already suspect.

posts.topic: Texas toll roads and how transplants get billed
posts.hook: Texas toll roads have no toll booths. Transplants find out from a letter.

deck.topic: Texas toll roads and how transplants get billed
deck.hook: Texas toll roads have no toll booths. Transplants find out from a letter.

points.title: Nobody Takes Your Money
body: Texas tollways read your plate at highway speed.
No tag means they mail the bill to whoever owns the car.
points.loop: That is the expensive option.

points.title: Get The Sticker
body: A toll tag is a free sticker for your windshield.
Tag rates are lower than mailed rates on the exact same road.
One tag covers Austin, DFW and Houston.
points.loop: Some days you skip it entirely.

points.title: The Free Road Beside It
body: Most Texas tollways have a free access road running right next to them.
Same direction, same exits, a few more traffic lights.
San Antonio drivers barely deal with tolls at all.
points.loop: One lane plays by different rules.

points.title: Austin Changes The Price
body: The express lanes in Austin do not charge a flat rate.
The price moves with traffic, so the worst hour costs the most.
points.loop: Then there is the car problem.

points.title: Rentals And Moving Trucks
body: The cameras do not care whose name is on the vehicle.
The rental company pays the toll, then bills you plus a daily fee.
points.loop: Ignoring one bill gets expensive fast.

points.title: Small Bills Grow Teeth
body: Unpaid tolls collect fees and late notices in the mail.
Enough of them can hold up your registration renewal.
points.loop: And it does not stop there.

cta.question: Toll road every day or free frontage road with the lights?

scores.worst_problem: The per-slide loops are mostly filler — "And it does not stop there," "That is the expensive option," and "One lane plays by different rules" either restate the slide or are too vague to name a payoff.
scores.fix: Rewrite every loop to tease a specific, concrete next fact (e.g. "Rental fees double it", "Austin prices move hourly", "It blocks your registration") instead of gesturing at more.

posts.topic: The long game of following up with buyers who said no
posts.hook: Half my closings this year came from people who told me no.

deck.topic: The long game of following up with buyers who said no
deck.hook: Half my closings this year came from people who told me no.

points.title: No Almost Never Means No
body: People say no when the timing is wrong, not when you are wrong.
The lease ends in June. The bonus lands in March. Dad moves in next fall.
points.loop: So I stopped counting the nos.

points.title: I Write Down The Date
body: Every no goes on a list with one date next to it.
The date is when their life changes, not when I feel like calling.
points.loop: Most of that list goes silent.

points.title: The Quiet Stretch
body: Nine to eighteen months of nothing back. No replies. No likes.
There is no sign anyone read a single word I sent.
points.loop: Then four of them called at once.

points.title: Four Calls, Six Weeks
body: Last spring four people off that list called inside six weeks.
Two had waited over a year. Not one of them interviewed another agent.
points.loop: That part was not luck.

points.title: Half My Closings
body: Add them up and half my closings this year started as a no.
I did not get better at selling. I just refused to delete anyone.
points.loop: Most people quit around month seven.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who deletes a lead the second they hear not right now.

scores.worst_problem: Two of the five loops ('So I stopped counting the nos.' and 'That part was not luck.') are reflective pivots rather than teases — they close the thought instead of dangling a specific unanswered thing.
scores.fix: Rewrite those two loops to name a withheld concrete object, e.g. 'So I started a list instead.' and 'They all had one thing in common.'

posts.topic: Texas builders are cutting payments, not prices, and what that hides in the comps
posts.hook: Texas builders are not cutting prices right now. They are cutting something else.

deck.topic: Texas builders are cutting payments, not prices, and what that hides in the comps
deck.hook: Texas builders are not cutting prices right now. They are cutting something else.

points.title: The Sticker Price Holds
body: Builders hate dropping the list price.
It upsets everyone who bought there last quarter, and it drags the appraisals down for the whole street.
points.loop: So the discount moves somewhere quieter.

points.title: It Goes Into The Loan
body: The money shows up as a rate buydown, closing costs covered, or upgrade credit instead.
Right now that package is often worth more than a price cut would have been.
points.loop: The paperwork hides it well.

points.title: The Comps Look Wrong
body: The sale records at full price. The incentive never lands in that number.
So the data says values are flat while the real cost to buy is lower.
points.loop: One group pays for that.

points.title: Resale Sellers Get Squeezed
body: You look at the numbers and think you can hold your price.
But the builder a mile away is beating you on the monthly cost, and you cannot buy down a buyer's rate. Price is your only lever.
points.loop: Buyers have a lever too.

points.title: Timing Moves The Number
body: Incentives get richest on finished homes still sitting at the end of a quarter.
What is posted online is the opening offer, not the best one.
points.loop: The best offers move weekly.

cta.payoff: the current new builds list, with what each one is paying in incentives this week

scores.worst_problem: Two of the five loops don't open anything forward — "The paperwork hides it well" just re-describes the slide's own point, and "The best offers move weekly" summarises the timing slide instead of teasing the close.
scores.fix: Rewrite those two loops to point at the next unknown — e.g. after the loan slide, "That breaks the price data"; after the timing slide, "Ask for the sitting inventory."

posts.topic: The three inspection windows on a Texas new build
posts.hook: You get three chances to inspect a Texas new build. Most buyers use zero.

deck.topic: The three inspection windows on a Texas new build
deck.hook: You get three chances to inspect a Texas new build. Most buyers use zero.

points.title: Code Is Not Quality
body: The city inspector works for the city, not for you.
He checks the legal minimum and moves on.
Passing means legal. It does not mean well built.
points.loop: Chance one closes before drywall.

points.title: Chance One: Pre Drywall
body: Once the walls close up, the wiring, pipes and framing are gone from view.
Your own inspector can walk it while everything is still open.
points.loop: Chance two is easy to waste.

points.title: Chance Two: The Walkthrough
body: The builder walks you through and writes a punch list before closing.
Bring your own inspector and that list gets a lot longer.
points.loop: Chance three has an expiry date.

points.title: Chance Three: Month Eleven
body: Most builder warranties on workmanship run one year.
Get inspected at month eleven, while they still have to fix it.
At month thirteen the repair bill is yours.
points.loop: None of this is free.

points.title: Who Pays For It
body: You hire the inspector yourself, a few hundred dollars per visit.
The builder cannot stop you from bringing one.
It is the cheapest money you will spend on the house.
points.loop: Six things they flag first.

cta.payoff: the new build inspection checklist I use at all three stages

scores.worst_problem: The final loop promises "Six things they flag first" — and the map bills "What gets flagged" as a section — but that slide never exists, so the deck's last open loop dead-ends into the CTA unpaid.
scores.fix: Either add the sixth slide listing the six most-flagged defects, or change the last loop to point at the checklist itself (e.g. "The list I hand my inspector").

posts.topic: Cedar fever in Austin and San Antonio
posts.hook: Transplants in Austin get sick every January. It is almost never the flu.

deck.topic: Cedar fever in Austin and San Antonio
deck.hook: Transplants in Austin get sick every January. It is almost never the flu.

points.title: It Is Cedar Pollen
body: Mountain cedar trees cover the Hill Country.
They dump pollen and it wrecks people. Chills, exhaustion, a stuffed head that feels like fever.
points.loop: The timing is what fools everyone.

points.title: Winter, Not Spring
body: This runs December through February.
Newcomers think allergy season means April, so they never connect the dots.
points.loop: Your address changes the dose.

points.title: Austin Gets It Worst
body: Austin sits right against the cedar. San Antonio catches plenty of it too.
DFW gets a much lighter version of the same thing.
points.loop: One weather pattern makes it brutal.

points.title: Blame The Cold Fronts
body: A front blows through, the wind swings around dry and cold.
That wind carries pollen off the hills in visible clouds.
points.loop: Most people react far too late.

points.title: Start Before It Starts
body: Locals begin their meds in late November, not after the first bad day.
Fresh air filters, windows shut, shower when you come in from outside.
points.loop: Locals argue about which is worse.

cta.question: Which would you rather ride out: cedar season or a Texas August?

scores.worst_problem: The final point slide's loop ("Locals argue about which is worse") doesn't grow out of that slide's content about starting meds early — it's a bolted-on bridge to the CTA rather than a tease of what's coming next.
scores.fix: Rewrite the last loop so it emerges from the prevention advice and genuinely sets up the debate (e.g. "Still, one season beats this"), and cut "Save this for later" so the closing question is the only ask.

posts.topic: The cash cushion after closing: why buyers get in trouble
posts.hook: The buyers who get in trouble in Texas almost never overpaid for the house.

deck.topic: The cash cushion after closing: why buyers get in trouble
deck.hook: The buyers who get in trouble in Texas almost never overpaid for the house.

points.title: Nobody Overpays Into Trouble
body: Almost every buyer I have watched struggle paid a fair price for a fine house.
They just closed with nothing left in the bank.
points.loop: The house asks first.

points.title: Month One Wants Money
body: Bare windows. No fridge, no fence, no blinds, no grass.
That list runs into the thousands before the boxes are unpacked.
points.loop: Then the mail arrives.

points.title: Year Two Sends A Bill
body: On a lot of new builds, the first tax bill is based on dirt.
The second one is based on the finished house, and your escrow has to catch up.
points.loop: Most people patch it the same way.

points.title: The 24 Percent Fence
body: Fence, furniture and the tax gap all land on credit cards.
The interest ends up costing more than the fence ever did.
points.loop: One habit prevents all of it.

points.title: Three Months, Untouched
body: After closing, keep three months of house payments sitting in cash.
Not invested. Not in the house. Just boring and available.
If that means buying under your approval number, buy under it.
points.loop: That cash does something else too.

points.title: It Buys You Time
body: People rarely sell at a loss because the market dipped.
They sell because a bad month showed up and there was no runway.
The cushion is what lets you wait the market out.
points.loop: You already know who needs this.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who is about to spend every dollar they have on the down payment.

scores.worst_problem: The first loop, "The house asks first," is cryptic enough that the reader has to decode it rather than crave the next slide, breaking the swipe chain at the earliest and most fragile point.
scores.fix: Rewrite loop one as a concrete tease of the immediate spend, e.g. "Move-in week costs thousands" or "The house bills you first," so every loop names a thing the reader wants to see.

posts.topic: Why the third price cut on a listing is the expensive one
posts.hook: On a Texas listing, the third price cut costs more than the first two combined.

deck.topic: Why the third price cut on a listing is the expensive one
deck.hook: On a Texas listing, the third price cut costs more than the first two combined.

points.title: Week One Is Everything
body: A fresh listing hits every saved search in the area at once.
Most homes get more showings in the first ten days than the next sixty.
points.loop: Then something quiet happens.

points.title: The Drop Off
body: After two weeks the new buyers have already seen it and passed.
Now the only thing growing is the days on market counter.
points.loop: Buyers read that number.

points.title: Chasing The Market
body: Most sellers cut a small amount and wait to see what happens.
The market keeps moving while you wait, so the new price is stale in three weeks.
points.loop: You are always one step behind.

points.title: Why Cut Three Hurts
body: By the third cut you have burned two months of calendar.
Buyers stop asking what the house costs and start asking what is wrong with it.
That is why cut three costs more than the first two combined.
points.loop: The calendar is not neutral.

points.title: The Month You List In
body: Buyer traffic in Texas is not the same in July as it is in March.
Pricing off what your neighbor got last spring is how the chase starts.
points.loop: Last year's numbers will fool you.

cta.payoff: this month's Texas market numbers, including how long homes are actually sitting before they sell

scores.worst_problem: Two of the five loops ('You are always one step behind.', 'Last year's numbers will fool you.') just restate the slide they close instead of pointing forward, so the swipe reason dies mid-deck.
scores.fix: Rewrite the loops on slides 3 and 5 to withhold the next slide's content — e.g. 'Cut three is the expensive one.' and 'There is a right month to list.'
